newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: New Zimbabwe Anglo Corp boss sees no problems.
newsitem.headline: New Zimbabwe Anglo Corp boss sees no problems.

text.p: Anglo American Corporation Zimbabwe's new chief executive said on Thursday he was excited about his appointment which President Robert Mugabe's government had earlier vowed to block on grounds it wanted a local black to fill the post.

"I am delighted to be coming...(and) I have been assured I will get a work permit," South African Philip Baum, who succeeds retiring Zimbabwean Roy Lander on October 1, told reporters at his first press briefing in Harare.

He said he would assume his post with an open mind, determined to ensure Anglo American Corporation Zimbabwe, a subsidiary of South African Anglo American, maintained its position as one of the southern African state's top conglomerates.
Baum, 42, was previously secretary to the executive committee of the South African parent Anglo American Corporation.

Answering questions on why the Zimbabwean government -- which had earlier this year vowed it wanted to see Lander succeeded by a black as part of its campaign to promote economic empowerment of majority blacks -- had allowed his appointment, he said:

"I think there is a political maturity on the floor and a relaisation of the roles both the private and the public sector need to play for business, social and economic development and how this partnership can work for the benefit of all," he said.
Baum denied Anglo Zimbabwe had bought his work permit by offering Mugabe's government an option to buy a 22 percent stake in its subsidiary Bindura Nickel Corporation BIND.Z.

The two signed an agreement on this three months ago, weeks after Mugabe had accused the corporation and other business groups of undermining efforts to empower blacks in an economy dominated by whites. Blacks outnumber whites 100-to-one in Zimbabwe.
"There is no connection whatsoever. There was no quid pro quo," Baum said.
Baum, who joined Anglo in 1979 and was also an alternate director of the corporation before his latest appointment, said he had a five-year term in Zimbabwe.

He did not know, he said, whether he would be succeeded by Elias Ngugama, 57, a black former chief executive of Bindura Nickel Corporation who was on Thursday appointed non-executive chairman of Anglo Zimbabwe with effect from next March.
"We are delighted to have him because he is highly respected in business. He is his own man, and I would be disappointed if he was judged on the basis of his colour," Baum said of Ngugama.
Ngugama, would, as non-executive chairman, have a "helicopter view of the corporation", and offer management crucial constructive criticism on behalf of shareholders, he said.
